"We're a team. No matter what happens out there, I've got your six."

This phrase is widely used among soldiers, police officers, and close friends to express deep, reliable support.
Tone and Register — When and Where Is It Used?

• Military and law enforcement — very common, used literally and seriously.
  • Action movies, TV shows, video games — extremely common, especially in war films, crime dramas, and military games.
  • Casual conversation among friends — used informally to mean "watch out" or "I've got your back."
  • Business or professional settings — used occasionally, as a slightly dramatic or colorful way of saying "stay alert."

The idiom carries a tough, serious, no-nonsense tone. It sounds confident and alert. It does not sound gentle or casual — it sounds like someone who knows what danger looks like and is taking it seriously.

One Final Way to Remember It

Here is the simplest way to lock this idiom in your memory forever:

Your eyes are at 12 o'clock. Your blind spot is at 6 o'clock. Watching your six means guarding the one place you can't naturally see.

That's the whole idea — simple, sharp, and built on a clock face. Once you see it that way, you'll never forget it.
15765:
A watchword is a word or short phrase that carries special importance — either as a secret signal used to verify identity, or as a guiding principle that defines what a person, group, movement, or era stands for.

These two meanings share a common thread: in both cases, the watchword is the word that matters most in a given context. It carries weight. People return to it again and again.
Meaning 1: A secret password or signal word

This is the older, more literal sense. Historically, guards and soldiers used a pre-arranged secret word to tell friend from foe. If someone wanted to pass through a checkpoint, they had to whisper the watchword — the right word that proved they were on the same side.

Think of it as a spoken key that unlocks trust.

Example: Before the raid, the commander told each soldier the watchword so they could identify one another in the dark.

This use is mostly tied to military history and historical fiction today. You won't hear it much in everyday modern conversation in this sense.
Meaning 2: A guiding principle or motto (the common modern use)

This is where the word lives and breathes today. A watchword in this sense is the single word or phrase that best captures what someone or something is all about — the idea they keep coming back to, the value they organize everything around.

It answers the question: "If you had to pick one word to describe what this group/movement/era/person is all about, what would it be?"

Examples:

  • "Efficiency was the watchword of the new management team."
    → Everything they did was driven by one goal: be efficient. That was their defining principle.
  • "For the reform movement, equality was the watchword."
    → Equality was the idea they rallied around, talked about constantly, and measured all their decisions against.
  • "In today's startup world, disruption is the watchword."
    → Disruption is the big idea everyone in that world keeps invoking.
  • "The watchword in this hospital is patient safety — every policy, every procedure, every decision flows from that."
    → Patient safety is not just one value among many; it's the master value.
The feel and tone of the word

A watchword is not just any important word. It carries a sense of declaration and commitment. When you call something a watchword, you're saying:

  • This word isn't decoration — it actively shapes behaviour and decisions.
  • It's the word people invoke repeatedly, almost ritually.
  • It defines the identity of a group or a time.

The word has a somewhat formal, serious tone. You'll find it often in journalism, political commentary, historical writing, and formal speeches — not so much in casual chat. If someone says it in conversation, they're usually making a deliberate, slightly elevated point.

This is important because several words overlap with it, and understanding the differences sharpens your grasp of what watchword uniquely means.

Watchword vs. Motto
A motto is an official, fixed statement — etched into a school crest, printed on a coat of arms, declared formally. It belongs to an institution and stays stable over time. A watchword is more dynamic and contextual — it describes the driving idea of a particular moment, person, or movement, not necessarily something officially adopted. A school has a motto; a new political campaign has a watchword.

Watchword vs. Slogan
A slogan is designed for the public — it's outward-facing, catchy, and meant to promote something. "Just Do It" is a slogan. A watchword is more inward-facing — it's the idea that guides how a group actually thinks and acts, not what they advertise to the world.

Watchword vs. Buzzword
A buzzword is a trendy, fashionable term that gets overused, often without much real meaning behind it. A watchword is earnest — it's meant to genuinely guide. Ironically, a word can start as a sincere watchword and degrade into a buzzword over time if it gets repeated emptily.

Watchword vs. Mantra
A mantra is usually personal — a phrase you repeat to yourself for motivation or focus. A watchword is typically collective — it belongs to a group, era, or movement. One person quietly repeating "I am enough" to themselves has a mantra. A reform movement publicly rallying around "accountability" has a watchword.

Watchword vs. Rallying cry
A rallying cry is emotional and calls people to action in the moment — it stirs and mobilizes. A watchword is more steady and philosophical — it's the underlying principle that outlasts the heat of any single moment.

Notice how native speakers use this word:

  • "[Word] is/was the watchword of [group or era]."
    → "Austerity was the watchword of that decade."
  • "[Group's] watchword is [word]."
    → "Their watchword is transparency."
  • "The watchword here is [word]."
    → "The watchword here is caution — we cannot afford mistakes."
    (This pattern means: the most important principle to keep in mind right now is...)
  • "[Word] became the watchword of [movement/era]."
    → "Innovation became the watchword of the digital age."
A quick summary to lock it in

Sense 1A secret password used by soldiers or guards to verify identity (mostly historical)
Sense 2The single word or phrase that defines the guiding principle of a person, group, movement, or era (the common modern use)

The two senses connect like this: just as a watchword once marked who you truly were (friend or foe), in modern use it still marks what something truly stands for at its core.

When you read or hear "watchword" today, the writer is almost always pointing to the defining idea — the one value or principle that everything else flows from.
15766:
To understand this phrase deeply, start with the image it comes from.

Imagine you have a glass of strong orange juice. It's too bitter, so you pour some water into it. Now it's weaker — less flavourful, less intense, less like the original thing. You have watered it down.

This is exactly what the phrase means, even when used about things that have nothing to do with liquid.
The Core Meaning

"Water down" means to make something weaker, less powerful, less effective, or less extreme — usually in a way that takes away from its original quality or impact.

When you water something down, the essence is still there, but it has been reduced, softened, or diluted. It is no longer as strong as it originally was.
Grammar: How the Phrase Works

"Water down" is a phrasal verb — a verb combined with a small word (here, "down") that together create a new meaning.

The different forms:

FormExample
  • Base form: water down → They will water down the plan.
  • Past tense: watered down → They watered down the plan.
  • Present continuous: watering down → They are watering down the plan.
  • Third person present: waters down → She always waters down her criticism.
  • Adjective form (very common!): watered-down → It was a watered-down version of the original.

Notice that "watered-down" with a hyphen is used as an adjective before a noun — this is one of the most common ways you will encounter this phrase in real life.
The Object Can Go in Two Places

When "water down" has an object (the thing being weakened), you can place it in two positions:

  • Water down + object: They watered down the proposal.
  • Water + object + down: They watered the proposal down.

Both are correct. However, if the object is a pronoun (it, them, this), it must go in the middle:

  • ✅ They watered it down.
  • ❌ They watered down it.
Real-World Meanings and Contexts

This phrase is used very widely. Here are the main areas of life where you'll hear and read it:

1. Laws and Policies

This is perhaps the most common use. When a government proposes a strict new rule but then reduces its strength — perhaps due to pressure from powerful groups — the rule has been "watered down."

"The anti-pollution law was watered down after heavy lobbying from the oil industry. The final version had very little real power."

The idea: the law started strong, like undiluted juice, but ended up weak and ineffective.

2. Plans and Proposals

When someone has an ambitious idea but is forced to reduce it, shrink it, or remove the bold parts:

"The architect's original design was stunning. But due to budget cuts, the final building was a watered-down version — plain, ordinary, and forgettable."

3. Criticism and Feedback

When someone softens their criticism to be polite, so the message loses its impact:

"She gave me watered-down feedback. She was too nice to tell me the truth, so I didn't learn anything useful."

4. Teaching and Explanations

When a complex subject is simplified so much that the real substance is lost:

"The textbook watered down the theory to the point where it no longer made sense."

Note: There is a difference between simplifying well (keeping the truth intact while making it accessible) and watering down (removing so much that the meaning suffers). "Water down" always implies the latter — a harmful reduction.

5. Food, Drinks, and Medicine

This is closer to the literal origin. A restaurant that adds too much water to their soup has watered it down. A dishonest shopkeeper who adds water to milk has watered it down.

"This coffee tastes terrible — they've watered it down completely."
The Tone and Connotation

"Water down" almost always carries a negative tone. It suggests:

  • Disappointment ("this isn't what it should have been")
  • Compromise that went too far ("they gave up too much")
  • Loss of quality or integrity ("the real thing has been harmed")
  • Sometimes, dishonesty or cowardice ("they didn't have the courage to keep it strong")

It is rarely used to describe a good thing. When someone says something was "watered down," they are almost always criticising it.
"Watered-Down" as an Adjective — Pay Attention to This

The adjective form "watered-down" is extremely common in writing and speech. It describes something that has already been weakened.

  • "This is a watered-down democracy — the elections exist, but have no real meaning."
  • "He gave a watered-down apology. He said sorry, but took no responsibility."
  • "We received a watered-down offer — far below what we asked for."

Every time you see "watered-down" before a noun, it is telling you: this thing looks like the real thing, but its power or quality has been significantly reduced.
The Opposite Idea

If "water down" means to weaken or dilute, then the opposite would be to strengthen, intensify, or keep intact. You might say:

  • "They kept the original proposal intact — they refused to water it down."
  • "She delivered her criticism in full, without watering it down."
Synonyms and Related Expressions

These words and phrases share a similar meaning to "water down," though each has its own nuance:

  • Dilute — very close in meaning; often used in formal or scientific contexts ("Don't dilute the message.")
  • Tone down — to make something less extreme or harsh ("Tone down your language.")
  • Soften — to make less harsh or severe, but often in a gentler, not necessarily negative way
  • Weaken — straightforward; to reduce strength
  • Gut — informal and stronger; to remove the most important parts of something ("They gutted the legislation." — even stronger than "watered down")
  • Hedge — to avoid being direct or clear; to soften a commitment
  • Sanitise (or sanitize) — to remove anything controversial, offensive, or real, leaving something clean but lifeless
A Subtle but Important Point

"Watering down" doesn't mean destroying something completely. It means reducing it while keeping the outer appearance. The thing still exists — there is still a law, still a plan, still a story — but its power has been drained away. This is what makes it such a vivid and expressive phrase. The watered-down version looks real but lacks substance.

This is why it's often used to describe political compromises, corporate decisions, and creative works that were changed to avoid controversy. The shell remains; the soul is gone.
Quick Summary

"Water down" means to weaken, dilute, or reduce the strength of something — whether it's a law, a plan, an idea, a speech, a criticism, or a drink. It comes from the literal act of adding water to a liquid to make it less strong. It almost always implies that something valuable has been lost in the process. The adjective form "watered-down" is very common and is used to describe anything that has been reduced from its original, full-strength form.
15767: "Watershed" has three distinct meanings — one literal (geographical), one extended from it (broadcasting), and one figurative (everyday language). A truly complete understanding of this word requires knowing all three.
Meaning 1: A Geographic Area (The Core, Literal Meaning)

A watershed is the entire area of land from which all water drains into the same river, lake, or sea.

Think of it this way: when it rains, the water doesn't just sit there. It flows downhill. Gravity pulls it along slopes, into streams, into rivers, and eventually into the sea. A watershed is the total land area that "feeds" a particular river or body of water — every drop of rain or melted snow that falls anywhere within that area will eventually find its way to the same destination.

Imagine holding a giant bowl upside down and pouring water over it. Every drop rolls down and off the bowl. The entire surface of that bowl is like a watershed — all the water that touches it drains the same way. Now imagine that bowl is made of mountains and valleys. The slopes, the hillsides, the flat plains — all of it belongs to one watershed if the water ultimately flows to the same river or lake.

Example: The Mississippi River watershed covers a massive area of North America — roughly 40% of the continental United States. Any rain that falls in that enormous region — whether in Montana or Pennsylvania — will eventually drain into the Mississippi River system.

Watersheds are separated from each other by ridges or high ground. These ridges act as natural dividing lines. Rain falling on one side of a ridge flows into one watershed; rain falling on the other side flows into a completely different one. These dividing ridges are sometimes called divides (as in the famous "Continental Divide" in North America).

Important note on regional usage: In American English, "watershed" almost always refers to the entire drainage area described above. In British English, however, "watershed" can also refer specifically to the ridge itself — the line of high ground that forms the boundary between two drainage areas — rather than the area it encloses. So depending on where you encounter the word, it may mean the "basin" (the area) or the "divide" (the boundary line). Both usages are correct; just be aware of the context.
Meaning 2: The Broadcasting Watershed (A Specific, Established Use)

In British broadcasting, the watershed (almost always used with the definite article "the") refers to 9 o'clock in the evening — the point in the broadcast day before which TV content must be suitable for children.

Before 9 PM, broadcasters are expected to show only content appropriate for a general audience, including young viewers. After 9 PM — post-watershed — channels are permitted to air programmes with more adult themes, stronger language, violence, or explicit content, since it is assumed children are less likely to be watching at that hour.

This meaning is a direct extension of the geographical meaning. Just as a physical watershed is a dividing line that determines which way water flows, the broadcasting watershed is a dividing line in time that determines which kind of content is permissible.

Example: "That documentary contained scenes not suitable for younger viewers, so it was scheduled after the watershed."

This usage is specifically British (and to some extent Irish). In American English, a similar concept exists but is described differently (terms like "safe harbor" are used instead, and the rules are structured somewhat differently).
Meaning 3: A Turning Point or Decisive Moment (The Figurative Meaning)

In everyday language, a watershed (or a watershed moment) refers to a critical point in time that marks a significant change — a turning point that clearly divides a "before" from an "after."

This figurative meaning flows naturally from the geographical one. Just as a physical watershed divides land into areas that drain in completely different directions, a figurative watershed divides time into two distinct periods that go in very different directions. Before the watershed moment, things were one way. After it, they are fundamentally different.

This meaning is extremely common and you will encounter it constantly in journalism, history, politics, and everyday conversation.

Examples:

  • "The invention of the internet was a watershed in human communication."
  • "The 2008 financial crisis was a watershed moment for global economic policy."
  • "That argument was a watershed in their relationship — things were never quite the same again."

Notice that a watershed moment is not just any important event. It is specifically one that divides — one that causes a clear and lasting shift in direction. The key idea is before vs. after, with a meaningful difference between the two.

All three meanings share the same core idea: a dividing line that determines direction.

  • In geography, it divides land and determines which way water flows.
  • In broadcasting, it divides the day and determines which content can air.
  • In figurative use, it divides time and marks a change in direction of events.

Once you see that central thread — a dividing line that changes direction — the word becomes very intuitive across all its uses.
