To wheeze means to breathe with a rough, noisy, whistling or rattling sound — the kind of sound that makes it obvious that breathing is difficult and effortful. It is not silent breathing. It is not even just loud breathing. It is breathing that produces a specific, somewhat musical but unpleasant sound — like air being pushed through a very narrow pipe or a partially blocked tube.

Think of a squeeze toy that makes a squeak when you press it. Now imagine that squeak happening inside someone's chest, every time they breathe in or out. That is very close to what wheezing sounds like.

Wheezing happens when the airways inside the lungs or throat become narrow, swollen, or partially blocked. Because the air has to squeeze through a tighter space than normal, it vibrates and creates that distinctive high-pitched or raspy noise.

Common causes include:

  • Asthma — the most well-known cause. The airways tighten up and make breathing very hard.
  • A bad cold or chest infection — mucus and inflammation narrow the air passages.
  • Allergies — things like dust, pollen, or pet hair can trigger it.
  • Old age or poor health — the lungs and airways weaken over time.
  • Heavy physical exertion — even a relatively healthy but very out-of-shape person might wheeze after running hard.

The key thing to understand is this: wheezing is always a sign that something is making breathing harder than it should be.
What It Sounds Like — More Precisely

The sound of wheezing is usually described as:

  • High-pitched and whistling — like a soft whistle or a hiss
  • Audible to others nearby — it is not just something the person feels; people around them can hear it
  • Rhythmic — it follows the person's breathing rhythm, so it comes and goes with each breath

It is most commonly heard when the person breathes out (exhales), though in severe cases it can also be heard when they breathe in.

The verb "wheeze" is flexible. Here are the main ways it appears:

1. To describe the act of breathing with difficulty:

  • "She wheezed all night because of her asthma."
  • "He was wheezing badly after climbing the stairs."
  • "The old man wheezed and coughed throughout the morning."

2. To describe speaking while having trouble breathing:
When someone is so out of breath that they can barely form words, you can say they wheezed what they said — meaning they spoke while struggling to breathe.

  • "'I can't... go any further,' he wheezed."
  • "She wheezed a thank-you before collapsing into the chair."

This usage shows that the person is so breathless that their words themselves come out broken, raspy, and labored.

3. To describe a machine or object making a similar sound:
This is a very common figurative extension of the word. When an old, worn-out, or struggling machine makes a labored rasping or hissing sound — as if it too is "struggling to breathe" — writers often say it wheezes. This gives the machine almost human-like qualities of exhaustion and age.

  • "The old car engine wheezed and sputtered before finally starting."
  • "The ancient air conditioner wheezed loudly in the corner."
  • "The elevator wheezed as it slowly climbed to the fifth floor."

In all these cases, the word is painting a picture: this machine is barely managing, it is old and tired, and the sounds it makes reflect that struggle.
The Feeling and Connotation the Word Carries

"Wheeze" is not a neutral word. It carries a strong emotional and sensory weight. When a writer chooses to use this word, they are doing several things at once:

  • Telling you that breathing is labored and painful to witness or experience
  • Suggesting weakness, age, illness, or exhaustion
  • Creating an auditory image — you almost hear the word itself
  • Sometimes conveying sympathy (for a sick person), or humor (for a ridiculous old machine struggling along)

It is a vivid, evocative word. A good author uses it because it says far more than simply "breathe heavily" or "struggle to breathe."

Not all wheezing is the same in intensity. The verb can describe:

  • Mild wheezing — a slight, soft whistling that only happens occasionally or after exertion
  • Moderate wheezing — noticeable and consistent, clearly heard by others
  • Severe wheezing — loud, constant, and frightening; the person may barely be able to speak or move

Context and surrounding words usually tell you how serious the wheezing is. Compare:

  • "He wheezed slightly as he caught his breath." → mild
  • "She wheezed desperately, clutching her inhaler." → severe

• Wheeze and cough — these two almost always appear together, since respiratory illness causes both.
  • Wheeze out — to say something with great effort while barely able to breathe ("She wheezed out a few words.")
  • Wheeze along — often used for machines, meaning to continue working but barely, with great difficulty ("The old bus wheezed along the mountain road.")

To wheeze is to breathe — or to move air — in a difficult, noisy, whistling or rasping way, because something is narrowing or blocking the airway. It tells you that breathing is a struggle, not something happening easily and silently. It applies to people who are ill, old, exhausted, or having an attack of asthma — and by extension, to old or broken machines that seem to be "gasping" along just like a struggling person would.
15796:
"When push comes to shove" means when a situation becomes serious enough that you are forced to act, decide, or face reality — even if you were avoiding it before.

It is used to describe that critical moment when things can no longer stay easy, vague, or comfortable. The "nice" options have run out. Now you have to do something real.

Think of it as the line between talking and doing, or between easy and hard. When push comes to shove, the easy part is over.

To understand any idiom well, it helps to picture what the words literally describe.

Imagine two people in a mild disagreement. One person gives the other a small push — it's annoying, but not serious. Things are tense, but manageable.

Now imagine that push is returned with a harder shove — now it's a real confrontation. The situation has escalated. It's no longer a minor irritation; it has become something that demands a response.

So the phrase captures a progression:

  • Push = a mild pressure, a small problem, a situation you can still handle casually
  • Shove = things have gotten serious, urgent, and unavoidable

"When push comes to shove" = when the mild pressure becomes a serious, unavoidable force.

The idiom most likely comes from physical sports and street confrontations, where pushing is a common first step in a conflict, and shoving signals that things have truly gotten out of hand. The phrase started appearing commonly in American English in the early-to-mid 20th century, and today it is used widely across the English-speaking world.

You may also hear a slightly different version: "if push comes to shove" — the meaning is exactly the same. The word "when" suggests it will happen; "if" suggests it might happen. Both are perfectly correct and common.

This idiom usually appears in two situations:

1. To describe what someone will truly do under pressure

People often say one thing when life is comfortable, but act differently when things get hard. This idiom is used to cut through the pretense and get to the truth.

"He says he doesn't care about money, but when push comes to shove, he'll take the higher-paying job."

Translation: When he's actually forced to choose, the truth about his values will come out.

2. To describe a backup plan or last resort

It can also signal that there's a final option available — something you'd only use when everything else has failed.

"We'd like to finish the project without extra funding, but when push comes to shove, we can apply for a loan."

Translation: If things get desperate enough, we have a last option we can fall back on.

Here are several examples across different life situations, so you can see the idiom working in many contexts:

  • Friendship: "She seemed unreliable, but when push came to shove, she was the first one to show up and help me."
  • Career: "I prefer working independently, but when push comes to shove, I can collaborate with anyone."
  • Parenting: "Parents might disagree on many things, but when push comes to shove, they both want what's best for their child."
  • Business: "The two companies had been rivals for years, but when push came to shove, they agreed to merge rather than both go bankrupt."
  • Personal values: "He talked a big game about being brave, but when push came to shove, he backed down."

Notice how in each case, the idiom marks a moment of truth — a point where reality takes over from comfortable assumptions.

This idiom often carries a slightly realistic or even skeptical tone. When someone uses it, they're often implying:

  • "Let's stop being idealistic and think about what will actually happen."
  • "Forget the comfortable version — what happens in the hard version?"

It's a grounding phrase. It brings a conversation back to reality.
Tense: "Push Came to Shove" vs. "Push Comes to Shove"

You will see this in two tenses:

  • "When push comes to shove" — talking about a hypothetical future situation, or a general truth. (Most common form.)
  • "When push came to shove" — talking about a specific past event where this moment of truth actually happened.

"When push came to shove, she found out who her real friends were." (Past — it already happened.)

Both are correct. The tense just depends on whether you're talking about something that might happen or something that already did.

To make sure there's no confusion:

  • It does not mean physical violence or an actual fight. It's entirely figurative.
  • It does not mean that the outcome was necessarily bad. The "shove" just means things got serious — the result could be positive or negative.
  • It does not only refer to conflict. It can apply to any situation — financial decisions, relationships, career choices, etc.

Knowing related idioms helps you understand where "when push comes to shove" fits in the English language:

  • "When the rubber meets the road" — when theory is tested by real action. Very similar in meaning.
  • "When it comes down to it" — when you strip away everything else and face the core truth.
  • "When the chips are down" — when the situation is at its most serious or desperate.
  • "At the end of the day" — when all is said and done, what truly matters.

All of these share the idea of cutting through the noise and reaching the moment of real importance. "When push comes to shove" is unique, though, in its strong image of physical escalation — it carries a more vivid, urgent energy than the others.

MeaningWhen a situation gets serious and forces you to act or reveal what you truly will do
ToneRealistic, grounding, sometimes slightly skeptical
Used forDescribing moments of truth, last resorts, or what someone will really do under pressure
Variants"If push comes to shove" / "When push came to shove"
RegisterInformal — common in everyday speech, acceptable in casual writing

"When push comes to shove" is about the gap between comfortable words and serious reality — and what happens when life forces you to cross that gap.
15797:
"Whence" means "from where."

That's the heart of it. Every time you see or hear "whence," mentally replace it with "from where" or "from which place," and the sentence will make perfect sense.

  • "Whence do you come?" = "From where do you come?"
  • "He returned to the village whence he had set out." = "He returned to the village from which he had set out."
The Word Always Carries "From" Inside It

This is the single most important thing to understand about "whence": the idea of "from" is already baked into the word. You don't need to add "from" before it. "Whence" doesn't just mean "where" — it specifically and always means from where.

Think of it this way:

  • Where — at/in what place
  • Whence — from what place (origin, source, starting point)

So if someone asks "Whence did the river flow?", they're asking about the river's source — the place it came from, not where it is now.
It Points to Origin and Source

"Whence" is used when you want to talk about where something originated or came from — a starting point, a source, a cause. It answers the question: "What is the origin of this?"

Examples:

  • "No one knew whence the stranger had come." (No one knew from what place the stranger had come — his origins were a mystery.)
  • "She returned to the land whence she was born." (She returned to the land from which she originated.)
  • "The light came from a room whence music could also be heard." (The light came from a room, and from that same room, music could be heard.)
It Works for Abstract Origins Too, Not Just Physical Places

"Whence" doesn't only refer to a physical location. It can also point to the source of an idea, a tradition, a feeling, a power — anything that has an origin.

  • "He questioned the authority whence those laws were derived." (He questioned the source from which those laws were derived — not a place, but an institution or system.)
  • "Wisdom is the spring whence good decisions flow." (Wisdom is the source from which good decisions originate.)
  • "Scientists studied the conditions whence life first emerged." (Scientists studied the conditions from which life first emerged — its origin in time and circumstance, not a specific room or city.)

So whenever something has a starting point — whether it's a journey, an idea, a tradition, a feeling, or a force — "whence" can point to that starting point.
A Common Point of Confusion: "From Whence"

You will very often encounter the phrase "from whence" in literature, the Bible, and older writing:

"I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." — Psalm 121

Strictly speaking, "from whence" is redundant because "whence" already means "from where" — adding "from" is like saying "from from where." However, this usage is so deeply embedded in classic literature and formal writing (Shakespeare, the King James Bible, legal documents) that it is universally understood and widely accepted. You will encounter it constantly when reading older or formal texts.

The rule of thumb:

  • In careful, modern formal writing: use "whence" alone (without "from").
  • When reading older or literary texts: "from whence" simply means "from where" — the "from" is just an old habit, ignore the redundancy and read it normally.
It Is Formal and Archaic — You Will Mostly Read It, Not Say It

"Whence" is not a word of everyday modern conversation. Almost no one says it in casual speech anymore. If you said "Whence did you come?" to a friend, they'd find it charmingly old-fashioned or theatrical.

You will encounter it in:

  • Classic literature (Shakespeare, Dickens, Milton, the Bible)
  • Legal and formal documents (laws, proclamations, official writing)
  • Philosophy and academic prose
  • Poetry and elevated literary writing
  • Formal speeches or rhetoric

In modern speech and informal writing, people simply say "where did you come from?" or "from where." But when reading texts from these domains, you will encounter "whence" frequently, and now you know exactly what it means.

What it meansfrom where; from which place; from what source or origin
What's built inThe word already contains the meaning of "from" — you don't need to add it
Works forPhysical places AND abstract sources (ideas, traditions, causes, power)
"From whence"Technically redundant, but accepted — found throughout classic literature
RegisterFormal, literary, archaic — you'll read it more than say it
One Final Example to Lock It In

Imagine a king addresses a knight who has arrived from a distant land:

"Tell me, knight — whence do you come, and whence comes the news you carry?"

He is asking two things: (1) What land/place are you from? and (2) What is the source/origin of this news you bring — who sent it, where did it come from?

Both uses — the physical origin of the person and the abstract source of the news — are captured by a single word: whence.
15798:
When someone asks "Where do you come down on [someone or something]?", they are asking:

"What is your final opinion, judgment, or position about this person or topic? Which side do you land on?"

It is a way of asking someone to declare their stance — to stop sitting on the fence and tell you what they actually think or believe.
The Picture Behind the Words (The Metaphor)

To truly understand an idiom, it helps to see the image behind it.

Imagine an old-fashioned weighing scale — the kind with two pans that tip up and down. When you are thinking about an issue or a person, your mind is like that scale, balancing the pros and cons. At some point, the scale tips — it "comes down" on one side. That moment of tipping is when you reach your final verdict.

The phrase "come down" captures exactly that moment: you were up in the air (undecided), and now you have come down — you have landed firmly on one side.

Similarly, think of a judge's gavel coming down with a loud bang. When the gavel comes down, the decision is made. There is no more wavering.

So when someone asks "where do you come down?", they are asking: "On which side has your scale landed? What has your gavel decided?"

Let's look at the full sentence structure:

"Where do you come down on [someone or something]?"

  • "Where" — this asks for a position, not a physical place. Think of it as asking "On which side? In which direction?"
  • "Come down" — this means to arrive at a firm position after some thought or deliberation
  • "On [someone or something]" — this tells you what the topic of the judgment is

This is the most classic use. The expression is very commonly used when there is a debate, a controversy, or two sides to an issue.

Examples:

  • "Where do you come down on the death penalty?"

(= What's your position? Are you for it or against it?)

  • "The team argued for an hour about the budget cuts. Where do you come down on it?"

(= After all the discussion, what is your opinion?)

  • "There are two very different proposals on the table. Where do you come down?"

(= Which proposal do you support?)

Notice that the question almost always implies there are at least two possible positions, and the speaker wants to know which one you have chosen.

Yes, the expression is also used when the subject is a person, not just a topic. In this case, it means: "What is your judgment of this person? Do you support them, trust them, oppose them, or condemn them?"

Examples:

  • "A lot of people have mixed feelings about the new mayor. Where do you come down on him?"

(= Do you think he is good or bad? Do you support or oppose him?)

  • "She has both loyal fans and harsh critics. Where do you come down on her as a leader?"

(= What is your overall verdict on her?)

  • "The jury deliberated for three days. Where did they come down on the defendant?"

(= What was their final judgment about the defendant?)

When used with a person, the question is essentially asking: "Is this person, in your judgment, worthy of support, criticism, trust, or blame?"
The Tone and Feel of the Expression

This expression has a deliberate, serious tone. It is not a casual, throwaway question. When someone asks you "where do you come down on this?", they are implying:

  1. This is a matter that requires a decision.
  2. You have probably already thought about it or heard both sides.
  3. They want your real, considered opinion — not a vague or wishy-washy answer.

It is the kind of question that signals: "Stop being neutral. Tell me what you actually think."
The Difference Between "Come Down On" and "Where Do You Come Down On"

Be careful — there is a related but different expression: "come down on someone" (without "where do you").

  • "Come down on someone" = to criticize, scold, punish, or pressure someone harshly.

Example: "The boss came down hard on him for missing the deadline."
(= The boss criticized or punished him severely.)

  • "Where do you come down on someone?" = What is your judgment or opinion about this person?

Example: "Where do you come down on the new CEO — is she doing a good job?"
(= What is your verdict on her performance?)

The "where do you" part transforms the meaning entirely. Without it, "come down on" is about applying pressure or criticism. With "where do you," it is simply asking for your position or opinion.
How to Spot It in Conversation

You will typically hear this expression:

  • In debates, discussions, or arguments where people are choosing sides
  • In political conversations ("Where do you come down on immigration?")
  • In legal or professional settings ("Where do you come down on the liability issue?")
  • In casual conversations about controversial people or topics ("Where do you come down on him after everything that's happened?")
  • When a decision has to be made and someone wants to know your vote or view

When someone asks you this question, they expect you to commit to a position. A good answer starts with clarity:

  • "I come down on the side of stricter rules, because..."
  • "Honestly, I come down against him — I think he handled it badly."
  • "I'm still torn, but if I had to come down somewhere, I'd say..."

QuestionWhat It's Really Asking
"Where do you come down on this issue?"What is your final stance on this topic?
"Where do you come down on this person?"What is your judgment or verdict on this person?

In one sentence: "Where do you come down on [X]?" means "After considering everything, what is your firm opinion or judgment about [X]?" It is asking you to stop being undecided, pick a side, and declare it.
15799:
"Whereupon" means "immediately after which" or "at which point."

It connects two events by telling you that the second event happened directly and promptly following the first one. It acts like a bridge between two moments in time.

Think of it this way: Event A happens. Whereupon — Event B follows right away.

"Whereupon" sits between two clauses. It introduces the second clause and tells the reader: this is what happened next, right after the thing I just told you.

She slammed the door, whereupon the entire room fell silent.

Break it down:

  • First event: She slammed the door.
  • "Whereupon" = "immediately after which" / "at that moment"
  • Second event: The entire room fell silent.

You could replace it and get the same meaning:

She slammed the door, immediately after which the entire room fell silent.
She slammed the door. At that point, the entire room fell silent.

"Whereupon" is simply a more elegant, compact way to say those things.
The Two Layers of Meaning It Carries

"Whereupon" does two things at once — and this is what makes it precise and powerful:

1. It signals sequence — the second thing happened after the first.

2. It often implies a direct connection — the second thing happened because of or in direct response to the first. The first event triggered the second.

This is the nuance that separates "whereupon" from a plain "and then." "And then" just lines up two events. "Whereupon" suggests the first event set the second one in motion.

The judge read the verdict, whereupon the defendant broke down in tears.

This doesn't just say crying happened after the verdict. It implies the verdict is what caused the crying — the two events are directly linked.

That said, this causal flavour is not always strong. Sometimes "whereupon" simply marks a crisp, immediate sequence without a strong causal claim. Context tells you which reading fits.

He issued the command, whereupon the soldiers began to march.

→ The command was given. Immediately in response, the soldiers started marching. The command directly produced the marching.

The old bridge gave way, whereupon the cart plunged into the river.

→ The bridge collapsed, and at that very moment — as a direct result — the cart fell in. There's a tight cause-and-effect link.

The CEO announced her retirement, whereupon the board scheduled an emergency meeting.

→ The announcement happened. Right after, and directly because of it, the board met. Their meeting was a response to her announcement.

He finished his final exam, whereupon he felt a great wave of relief wash over him.

→ Here the connection is more psychological. Finishing the exam immediately brought on the feeling of relief. The sequence is tight and the link is clear.
The Feeling and Register of the Word

"Whereupon" is a formal word. It belongs to careful, literary, or official writing. You will encounter it in:

  • Literature and classic novels
  • Legal and official documents
  • Formal journalism and essays
  • Historical writing and biographies
  • Courtroom transcripts

You would not use it in everyday casual speech. Nobody says, "I opened the fridge, whereupon I discovered we were out of milk." That would sound stiff and out of place. In speech, you'd simply say "and then" or "at which point."

But in writing — especially when you want to give a sequence a sense of gravity, consequence, or formality — "whereupon" is a very clean and precise choice.
How It Differs from Similar Words

"Then" / "and then" — just marks a sequence. No implication of immediacy or direct connection.

He left, and then it started raining. (casual; the rain may be unrelated)

"Whereupon" — marks immediate sequence with a sense of direct response or consequence.

He left, whereupon it started raining. (slightly implies the rain came right as he left; the two events feel linked — perhaps dramatically so)

"Thereafter" — means "after that point," but without the sense of immediacy. It can refer to something that happened much later.

He moved abroad and thereafter rarely visited. (could be years later)

"Whereupon" is always about something that happens right then — without delay.

"Following which" / "after which"** — these are the closest plain-language equivalents of "whereupon." They are also formal but feel slightly more bureaucratic and less elegant.

"Whereupon" almost always comes mid-sentence, connecting two clauses with a comma before it. It is rarely used to start a sentence on its own. The structure is almost always:

[First event], whereupon [second event].

The king raised his hand, whereupon silence fell across the hall.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

What it means"Immediately after which" / "at which point"
What it doesConnects two events; shows the second happened right after — and often directly because of — the first
Key qualityImmediacy + a sense of direct connection or consequence
RegisterFormal — for writing, not casual speech
Structure[Event A], whereupon [Event B].

The word is richer than it looks. It's not just a fancy "then" — it carries a sense that the world shifted at that moment, and something happened right away as a result. That's the soul of "whereupon."
